units.objective: After this, a child can sort water as solid ice or liquid water when it is warmed or cooled, shown by a first-try tap on the matching picture.
units.why: The ice pop is hard in the cold and drips when the room is warm. What changed it?
useElsewhere: geography: glaciers and sea ice on the globe

units.objective: After this, a child can predict that warming ice makes liquid water and cooling that water makes ice again, shown by a first-try tap before the picture plays.
units.why: The puddle was ice this morning and water at lunch. Can it turn back into ice?
useElsewhere: everyday: freezing a drink on screen so it stays cold

units.objective: After this, a child can sort materials by color, texture, hardness, or flexibility, shown by a first-try sort of on-screen samples.
units.why: Two spoons look the same until you notice one bends and one does not. Which property did you use?
useElsewhere: everyday: picking a material you can see for a job on screen

units.objective: After this, a child can predict whether a magnet pulls a material without touching it, shown by a first-try tap before the magnet moves.
units.why: A pile of bits looks the same. Which ones will jump to the magnet?
useElsewhere: physics: a magnet sorting metals on screen

units.objective: After this, a child can take an on-screen model apart and build a new shape from the same pieces, shown by using every piece and adding none.
units.why: The bridge model is too short. Can the same pieces make a longer one?
useElsewhere: math: counting the same pieces in a new build

units.objective: After this, a learner can predict that salt on ice makes the ice melt at a temperature where plain ice would stay frozen, shown by a first-try tap before the road scene plays.
units.why: The road is icy. Crews spread salt. Why does the ice change? Fit: no exact code; MS-PS1-4 is the nearest.
useElsewhere: economics: the cost of keeping a road usable, as a plain money fact

units.objective: After this, a learner can pick the model that says a dissolved solid is still there as pieces too small to see, shown by a first-try choice. The scene does not ask anyone to taste it.
units.why: The solid in the glass picture is gone from sight. Is it gone, or still there?
useElsewhere: geography: salt seas and lakes on the globe

units.objective: After this, a learner can predict that the total weight stays the same when the on-screen substances are heated, cooled, or mixed, shown by reading the before-and-after scale.
units.why: The mix looks different. Did any of it disappear, or does the scale still match?
useElsewhere: economics: a shop batch weighs the same before and after, on screen

units.objective: After this, a learner can predict whether adding or removing warmth turns water among solid, liquid, and gas, shown by a first-try choice of the particle picture.
units.why: The kettle picture goes from ice, to water, to invisible water vapour above the spout. What did the warmth change?
useElsewhere: physics: particles moving faster when something is warmed

units.objective: After this, a learner can order an on-screen path of water as ice or liquid, into the air, into a cloud, and back as rain or snow, shown by a correct picture order.
units.why: The puddle disappeared and the sky has a cloud. Where did the water go, and how does it come back?
useElsewhere: geography: clouds, rain, and ice on the globe

units.objective: After this, a learner can predict whether an on-screen mix keeps the old look or shows a new one, shown by a first-try tap before the scene plays.
units.why: A shop counter on the screen stirs two plain substances. The picture may bubble. Is that still the same stuff?
useElsewhere: economics: a shop measures a drink mix on screen

units.objective: After this, a learner can compare a metal's look before and after rain and say the properties changed, shown by a first-try choice that a reaction may have happened.
units.why: A metal bike sat out in the rain. It looks different. Did the material change?
useElsewhere: economics: repair and replacement costs, as a plain money fact

units.objective: After this, a learner can identify a material by properties they observe, including whether it dissolves, shown by a first-try name from the on-screen tests. Floating is not scored.
units.why: Three unmarked blocks could be three different materials. Which test tells them apart?
useElsewhere: everyday: whether a solid disappears into water, on screen

units.objective: After this, an adult learner can predict that a warmer mix, or a more crowded one, changes how fast a reaction runs, shown by a first-try choice of which glow stick fades first.
units.why: Two glow sticks are the same, but one sits in warm water and one in ice water. Which one fades first, and why? Fit: adult extension of HS-PS1-5; no code covers beyond grade 12.
useElsewhere: everyday: a warmer on-screen mix finishes sooner

units.objective: After this, an adult learner can show that the count of atoms, and so the mass, matches on both sides of a simple on-screen reaction, shown by a balanced tally.
units.why: A simple reaction on the screen changes the look. Count the pieces on each side. Did any piece vanish? Fit: adult extension of HS-PS1-7; no code covers beyond grade 12.
useElsewhere: math: the same tally as a proportion, on a simple reaction only

units.objective: After this, an adult learner can revise a prediction for a simple main-group reaction drawn as a tally, using the periodic pattern, shown by a first-try revision. Iron rust is not the example: the page limits assessment to main-group elements and combustion.
units.why: The tally on the screen does not match the first guess. Which column pattern explains it? Fit: adult extension of HS-PS1-2; no code covers beyond grade 12.
useElsewhere: physics: energy in or out of a reaction, on screen, with no flame demo

chemistry:states:solid-liquid.prompt: An ice pop is hard in the cold and drips when the room is warm. What changed it?
chemistry:states:solid-liquid.derivation: Warmth changed the solid ice pop into a liquid: heating melted it.

chemistry:states:melt-freeze.prompt: A puddle was ice this morning and water at lunch. Tonight turns cold again. What can the water turn back into?
chemistry:states:melt-freeze.derivation: Cooling the water can freeze it back into ice — this change can be reversed.

chemistry:materials:sort.prompt: Two spoons look the same, but one bends and one does not. Which property tells them apart?
chemistry:materials:sort.derivation: The spoons were sorted by flexibility — whether the material bends.

chemistry:materials:magnet.prompt: A pile of bits looks the same. Which ones will jump to the magnet?
chemistry:materials:magnet.derivation: A magnet pulls iron, but it does not pull wood or plastic.

chemistry:pieces:rebuild.prompt: The bridge model is too short. Can the same pieces make a longer one?
choices: Yes — rebuild it longer with the same pieces
No — short pieces can never make a longer bridge
Only if you add new pieces
chemistry:pieces:rebuild.correct: Yes — rebuild it longer with the same pieces
chemistry:pieces:rebuild.derivation: The same pieces can make a new shape — take the model apart and rebuild it, using every piece and adding none.

chemistry:states:road-salt.prompt: Crews spread salt on an icy road. What does the salt do to the water in the ice?
choices: It lowers the freezing point of the water
It warms the road like a heater
chemistry:states:road-salt.correct: It lowers the freezing point of the water
chemistry:states:road-salt.derivation: Salt is a deicer: it lowers water's freezing point, so the ice melts at a temperature where plain ice would stay frozen.

chemistry:mixtures:dissolve.prompt: A solid stirred into water disappears from sight. Where did it go?
choices: It is still there, as pieces too small to see
chemistry:mixtures:dissolve.correct: It is still there, as pieces too small to see
chemistry:mixtures:dissolve.derivation: Dissolving breaks the solid into pieces too small to see — the substance is still in the water.

chemistry:reactions:weight.prompt: Substances are mixed on a scale and the mix looks different. What happens to the total weight?
chemistry:reactions:weight.derivation: Heating, cooling or mixing does not make matter vanish: the total weight stays the same.

chemistry:states:particles.prompt: The kettle picture goes from ice, to water, to invisible water vapour above the spout. What did the warmth change?
choices: The water, from solid to liquid to gas
chemistry:states:particles.correct: The water, from solid to liquid to gas
chemistry:states:particles.derivation: Warmth changes water from solid ice to liquid water to invisible water vapour.

chemistry:water:cycle.prompt: The puddle disappeared and the sky has a cloud. Where did the water go, and how does it come back?
choices: Into the air, a cloud, back as rain or snow
Down into the ground, where it stays for good
chemistry:water:cycle.correct: Into the air, a cloud, back as rain or snow
chemistry:water:cycle.derivation: The water went up into the air, into a cloud, and comes back as rain or snow.

chemistry:reactions:new-look.prompt: A shop counter stirs two plain substances. The picture may bubble. Is that still the same stuff?
choices: It might be a new substance
It is certainly the same stuff
It is certainly a new substance
chemistry:reactions:new-look.correct: It might be a new substance
chemistry:reactions:new-look.derivation: Mixing may make a new substance with different properties — a new look can mean a reaction happened.

chemistry:reactions:rust.prompt: A metal bike sat out in the rain. It looks different. Did the material change?
choices: Yes — iron exposed to oxygen and water turns to rust
No — rain only makes it look wet
chemistry:reactions:rust.correct: Yes — iron exposed to oxygen and water turns to rust
chemistry:reactions:rust.derivation: Iron becomes rust when it is exposed to oxygen and water — the metal itself changed.

chemistry:materials:identify.prompt: Three unmarked blocks could be three different materials. Which test tells them apart?
choices: Whether each block dissolves in water
chemistry:materials:identify.correct: Whether each block dissolves in water
chemistry:materials:identify.derivation: A material can be told apart by its properties — here, whether it dissolves in water.

chemistry:reactions:rate.prompt: Two glow sticks are the same. One sits in warm water, one in ice water. Which one fades first?
chemistry:reactions:rate.derivation: Warmer reacting particles react faster, so the warm-water glow stick uses itself up and fades first.

chemistry:reactions:mass.prompt: A simple reaction changes how the substances look. You count the atoms on each side of the tally. What does the count show?
choices: The same count on both sides — no atom vanished
chemistry:reactions:mass.correct: The same count on both sides — no atom vanished
chemistry:reactions:mass.derivation: Atoms are conserved in a reaction, so the count — and the mass — matches on both sides.

chemistry:reactions:explain.prompt: Two elements sit in the same column of the periodic table. One reacts with oxygen in a known way. What does the column pattern predict about the other?
choices: It reacts in a similar way
It turns into the first element
chemistry:reactions:explain.correct: It reacts in a similar way
chemistry:reactions:explain.derivation: Elements in the same column share outer-electron patterns, so they react in similar ways.
